extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and cautions for designing stable republican or confederate governments (lessons from ancient Greek republics), focusing on balance of powers, composition of assemblies, dangers of fragmentation, and measures to prevent factional violence and foreign intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced tripartite government with mutual negatives
rubrics_metrics.description: “Governed by a legislature composed of a king, senate, and assembly, with equal authority, and each a decisive negative.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that a mixture of three independent powers (king, senate, assembly), each with a veto/negative, is the only effective means to prevent the crumbling of liberty and to stop ambitious negotiators or ambassadors from embroiling the state. Repeatedly emphasized: “nothing has ever been found to supply the place of the balance of three powers.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Cities/towns must have internally mixed governments
rubrics_metrics.description: “The cities represented in [a congress] should have been well constituted of a mixture of three independent powers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a confederacy to function, constituent towns must themselves possess balanced (mixed) constitutions; otherwise a diplomatic assembly cannot check ambition or govern foreign affairs effectively. Example: Achaia’s congress might have governed well if member cities had internal balances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve small towns by union and common interest
rubrics_metrics.description: “Small cities could be preserved by nothing else but a continual and combined force, united by the bond of common interest.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted from Plutarch (as reported): dismemberment/independence of many small towns leads to decay; linked confederation (‘one great body’) preserves them. Anti-pattern: permitting towns to be separated into independent states leads to weakening and eventual ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid multiplication/division of states (extreme fragmentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning against letting every town become a free, sovereign, and independent democracy — this leads to wars, combinations, and intrigues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts Turgot’s idea (many tiny independent states) with historical Greek outcomes: fragmentation invites internal war, shifting alliances, external interference, and political instability. Practical implication: do not scale sovereign units down to tiny, economically weak towns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent factions from inviting foreign patrons
rubrics_metrics.description: When parties (monarchical, aristocratical, democratical) lack a balanced internal system, they will seek external aid (kings, Sparta, Macedon), producing cycles of violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes each Greek faction applied to a different external power for support; design must prevent domestic factions from appealing to foreign garrisons or princes. Anti-pattern examples: aristocrats appealing to Sparta, royalists to Macedon, democrats to other leagues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive control over negotiation can reduce foreign intrigue
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the power of negociation and treaties, and the whole executive, had been in one man... could the perfidious ambassadors... have intrigued?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim that concentrating treaty-making/executive authority in a single accountable official may reduce the scope for pernicious ambassadorial deals and foreign manipulation. This is presented as a counterpoint to purely legislative/executive fragmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotation of executive offices and accountability checks ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: Appointment of presidents in rotation and generals who are responsible to the congress (members responsible to their cities) checks ambition and preserves independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achaia’s practice of rotating praetorships and holding generals accountable to the assembly is praised as an institutional check on ambition. Practical measures: short terms, rotation, and clear responsibility/accountability to representative bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-assembly governments are vulnerable to capital dominance and breakup
rubrics_metrics.description: Republics governed by a single assembly (e.g., Biscay, Appenzell, underwald) saw subordinate towns complain of the inordinate influence of the capital and tended toward disunion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments by a single assembly that aggregate several towns without internal checks produce resentment of subordinate communities and are liable to dismemberment. Design implication: guard against dominant-capital capture of confederal institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design institutions to check domination by powerful capitals
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaint in many Greek states that a powerful capital domineered over inferior towns; good systems must check that domination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical institutional options include equitable representation, rotating presidencies, common laws/weights/measures, and limits on capital's unilateral authority. Example: Achaia’s equal treatment of towns is praised despite imperfections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for economic/fiscal capacity when assessing small-state viability
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek towns could wage war cheaply because of social structure; modern republics need sufficient money to support soldiers and diplomacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cautions that American towns differ materially (costs of war, soldiers’ pay, circulating medium). Designing governance must consider fiscal resources and economic means to sustain defense and diplomacy; lacking this, small independent states are impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider social structure (free citizens vs. slaves) before transplanting institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Greece often had forty slaves per town and one free citizen doing little but fighting; Americans must not uncritically transplant Greek models without considering differences in slavery and civic composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional recommendations must reflect demographic and social realities; the text satirically shows how Turgot’s idea would necessitate a harsh social division (determining freemen vs. slaves by lot), underscoring the need to adapt models to local social conditions.
